timeline.title: How the World Remembers
items: The Egyptians believed that saying someone's name out loud kept their memory alive. We think they were right.
Photography was announced to the world, and families could finally keep the faces of the people they loved.
On the first Armistice Day, people across Britain stopped for two minutes to remember. The tradition carries on.
In Mexico, families build bright altars with photos and favourite foods on the Day of the Dead, to welcome memories home.
today: Not in the history books. But written on every one of our hearts.

letters.title: What the World Has Said About Love and Memory
items: To live in hearts we leave behind is not to die.
Unable are the Loved to die, for Love is Immortality.
What we have once enjoyed we can never lose. All that we love deeply becomes a part of us.
Those we love never truly leave us.
letters.hand: They all say it beautifully. We just say: we love you, {who}.

facts.title: The Science of Remembering
items: Smell is wired close to the brain's memory centres, so one scent can bring a person right back to us.
The songs we love are some of the longest lasting memories we have. A tune can return a whole afternoon.
Studies have found that writing about the people we miss can help us feel a little lighter.
Some of the starlight we see tonight left its star long ago, and it is still reaching us. A little like love.
Elephants have been seen returning to gently touch the bones of family members, years later.
Sharing happy stories about someone we miss can genuinely lift our mood, and keeps them close.
facts.hand: Science can explain a lot. It cannot explain how much we miss you, {who}.

world.close: The world was better because of you, {who}. Ours most of all.

note.title: What we believe love is
paras: We make magazines for a living, but some feel different. This was one of them.
We believe a life is not measured in years. It is the hugs at the door, the stories at the table, the advice we still hear in our heads, and the people who carry it all forward.
{who}, your family wanted you to have something special. Not a card that goes in a drawer, but pages full of you: your words, your laughter, the little things that made you, you.
That someone is {from}. And from everything they told us, you were loved more than words could ever say.
